subject: Back Pay
title: PERC BP-2015-011 Final Order (Back Pay)
text:
STATE OF FLORIDA
PUBLIC EMPLOYEES RELATIONS COMMISSION
MARK ALSTON,
Employee, Case No. BP- 2015 -011
(Relates to CS- 2015 -032)
v.
FINAL ORDER
DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS,
: Order Number: 15CS -157
Date Issued: October 19, 2015
Agency.
Michael Braverman, Fort Lauderdale, attorney representing employee.
Sena M. Bailes, Tallahassee, attorney representing agency.
On June 30, 2015, the Public Employees Relations Commission (Commission)
issued an order vacating Mark Alston's dismissal by the Department of Corrections
(Agency). The Agency was directed to reinstate Alston and to provide him with back pay
and benefits, less any compensation and earnings which he would not have received
had his employment with the Agency not been interrupted. On the same date, this back
pay case was established. On July 15, a hearing officer was appointed to determine the
amount of back pay and an evidentiary hearing was scheduled.
On September 1, a telephone hearing was conducted between Tallahassee and
West Palm Beach. On September 16, the hearing officer issued his recommended order
concluding that Alston is entitled to gross back pay in the amount of $7,721.12, minus
taxes and other lawful deductions, plus $1,797.76 for health insurance costs. Neither
party filed exceptions to the hearing officer's recommended order or a transcript of the
back pay hearing.

BP-2015-011
(Relates to CS-2015-032)
We accept the hearing officer's findings of fact. Furthermore, we agree with the
hearing officer's analysis of the dispositive legal issues, his conclusions of law, and his
recommendations. Therefore, the hearing officer's recommended order is incorporated
herein. § 120.57(1)(1), Fla. Stat. (2015).
Based on the foregoing, the Agency is directed to pay Alston back pay in the
amount of $7,721.12, minus appropriate deductions, plus $1,797.76 for health insurance
costs, plus interest at the lawful rate until paid. Accordingly, this back pay case is closed.
This order and the Commission's June 30, 2015, Order Vacating Agency Action
may be appealed to the appropriate district court of appeal. A notice of appeal must be
received by the Commission and the district court of appeal within thirty days from the
date of this order. Except in cases of indigency, the court will require a filing fee and the
Commission will require payment for preparing the record on appeal. Further
explanation of the right to appeal is provided in Sections 120.68 and 447.504, Florida
Statutes (2015), and the Florida Rules of Appellate Procedure.
It is so ordered.
DELGADO and POOLE, Commissioners, concur.

MORTON, Hearing Officer.
On June 30, 2015, the Commission issued an order directing the Department of
Corrections (Agency) to reinstate Mark Alston and provide him with back pay and
benefits, less any compensation and earnings he would not have received had his
employment with the Agency not been interrupted. See Alston v. Department of
Corrections, Order No. 15CS -106 (PERC 2015). The Commission's Clerk opened a back
pay case based on the Commission's order. On July 8, Alston filed his computation of
back pay on PERC Form 18.
On September 1, after due notice and without objection, a telephone hearing was
conducted between Tallahassee and West Palm Beach. All parties were afforded the
opportunity to call witnesses, cross -examine witnesses, and fully participate.' Alston
entered one exhibit into evidence and he testified on his own behalf. The Agency did not
'This case was consolidated for hearing with Lawrence Young v. Department of
Corrections, BP- 2015 -010. While the underlying disciplinary cases were based on the
same occurrences, for purposes of clarity, I am issuing separate back pay recommended
orders.

BP-2015-011
(Relates to CS-2015-032)
offer any exhibits or witness testimony. The parties filed written post hearing arguments,
which I have carefully considered in preparing this recommended order. A transcript of
the hearing was not filed.
During the hearing, the parties arrived at a number of stipulated facts, which I have
included in my findings of fact below. The material dispute of fact necessitating the
hearing revolved around how much back pay Alston was entitled to receive and whether
he should be reimbursed for the out -of- pocket costs he paid to obtain health insurance.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Based on the record as a whole, I make the following findings:
1. Alston was terminated effective February 25, 2015. The Commission
issued its Order Vacating Agency Action on June 30. Alston returned to duty with the
Agency on July 17. The total back pay exposure period is February 25, 2015, through
and including July 16, 2015. (Stipulation)
2. Prior to his dismissal, Alston was employed as a Correctional Probation
Supervisor in the West Palm Beach Circuit Office.
3. Alston worked an eight hour workday /forty hour workweek schedule. His
gross wages were $23.54 hourly or $1,882.79 bi- weekly. (Stipulation)2
2There is a slight discrepancy between the bi- weekly amount calculated from the
hourly amount and the stipulated bi- weekly amount. ($23.54 per hour x 40 hours a week
x 2 weeks = $1,883.20 verses stipulated bi- weekly amount of $1,882.79). Because the
calculations include partial weeks and the need to consider daily amounts, I have used
2

BP-2015-011
(Relates to CS-2015-032)
4. The initial grace period lasted from February 25, through and including
March 26. (Stipulation)3
5. Alston did not take a disbursement from the Florida Retirement System and
he is eligible for reinstatement in the Florida Retirement System. (Stipulation)
6. There were twenty -two work days during the initial grace period. Alston is
entitled to $4,143.04 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions, for
the initial grace period.
7. Alston is also entitled to back pay for the second grace period, which
started on June 30, when the Commission entered its Order Vacating Agency Action and
July 17, when he returned to work. June 30 was a Tuesday, so Alston is also entitled to
receive back pay for Monday, June 29, pursuant to recent changes in Commission case
law.4
8. There were fourteen work days during the second grace period. Alston is
entitled to $2,636.48 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions, for
the second grace period.
the stipulated hourly amount in making my calculations. Any difference between the two
is negligible.
Pursuant to well -established case law, an employee is not required to seek
alternative work for the first thirty days after his or her dismissal. Sabria v. Department of
Business and Professional Regulation, 15 FCSR 682 (2000). This is commonly referred
to as the initial grace period.
41n Vickery v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 79 (2015), the Commission
held that an employee is entitled to back pay for the entire week in which the Commission
issues the order reinstating the employee to agency employment.
3

BP-2015-011
(Relates to CS-2015-032)
9. Alston did not have another job nor did he seek employment during the
back pay exposure period.
10. For the portion of the back pay exposure period from March 27 through
June 29, which covers sixty -seven work days, Alston is required to provide evidence that
he is entitled to back pay. Typically, this is demonstrated by providing evidence that an
employee conducted a good faith job search. During the initial discussions at hearing,
Alston's counsel stated that he did not conduct a job search. However, during his
testimony, Alston stated that he applied for a job as an adult protective investigator with
the Department of Children and Families. Alston interviewed for the position on May 14.
At the interview, Alston was asked if he was still working for the Agency and he told them
that he had been dismissed. Alston was not hired.
11. Alston is entitled to an additional $941.60, minus taxes and any other lawful
deductions, which represents one work week (five days) attributable to his attempt to get
a job with the Department of Children and Families.
12. Alston was provided health insurance coverage while he was employed by
the Agency. After he was terminated, his Agency -provided health care coverage lapsed
as of March 31.
13. Alston was required by federal law to obtain health insurance coverage for
his family or face tax penalties.
14. Alston purchased health insurance from Humana. His premium was
$449.44 per month.
4

BP-2015-011
(Relates to CS-2015-032)
15. Alston purchased health insurance for four months, April, May, June, and
July 2015.
16. Alston's total cost for health insurance during the back pay period was
$1,797.76.
ANALYSIS
In a back pay proceeding, the Commission is required to approximate the earnings
an employee would have received absent his improper discharge. See Florida State
Lodge, Fraternal Order of Police v. Town of Pembroke Park, 10 FPER IT 15001 (1983),
recon. denied, 10 FPER 1115072 (1984), affd in pertinent part, 501 So. 2d 1294 (Fla.
4th DCA 1987).
The parties reached stipulations on many of the variables necessary to calculate
the amount of Alston's back pay compensation, such as his rate of pay, work schedule,
and the starting and ending dates for his two grace periods. For the initial grace period,
Alston is entitled to $4,143.04 in gross back pay, less taxes and any other lawful
deductions. For the second grace period, Alston is entitled to $2,636.48 in gross back
pay, less taxes and any other lawful deductions.
While his attorney initially stated that he would not try to demonstrate a good faith
job search, Alston credibly testified that he applied for at least one job with another state
agency during the back pay period. Therefore, he is entitled to an additional $941.60,
5

(Relates to CS-2015-032)
minus taxes and any other lawful deductions. Consequently, Alston should be paid
$7,721.12 in gross back pay, minus taxes and other lawful deductions.
As for Alston's out -of- pocket insurance costs, at hearing, the Agency suggested
that Alston may not be entitled to any recovery of the amount he spent on health
insurance. However, the Commission has held that employees are entitled to
reimbursement for health insurance coverage as a component of back pay. See Miron v.
Amalgamated Transit Union, Local 1593, 34 FPER 11268 (2007) (citing Stanfield v.
Department of Health and Rehabilitative Services, 9 FCSR 11196 at 815 (1994)); see also
Smith v. Department of Corrections, 41 FPER 11202 (2014). In its post- hearing filing, the
Agency suggests that any amount awarded to Alston for health insurance should be
reduced by the amount of insurance that would have normally been taken out of his
paycheck had he continued to be employed by the Agency.5 However, the Agency did
not provide any evidence of what this amount might be or establish that Alston paid any
amount toward his Agency -provided health insurance. In the absence of these facts,
I
am inclined to award Alston the full amount that he paid toward health insurance during
the time he was out of work. As the Commission stated in its recent decision in Vickery
v. Department of Corrections, 30 FCSR 79 (2015), back pay proceedings are remedial in
nature and reasonable doubts should be resolved in favor of the employee because it
was the employer's wrongful conduct that initially caused the loss of employment.
5This suggestion is based on evidence that was offered regarding employee
Lawrence Young in Case No. BP- 2015 -010.
6

BP-2015-011
(Relates to CS-2015-032)
Therefore, Alston is entitled to be compensated for the $1,797.76 he spent on health
insurance during the back pay period.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. Alston is entitled to $7,721.12 in gross back pay wages, minus taxes and
other lawful deductions.
2. Alston is entitled to $1,797.76 to cover the amount he spent on health
insurance during the back pay period.
RECOMMENDATION
I recommend that the Commission adopt the foregoing recommended order and
award Alston back pay and benefits as set forth above.
Any party may file exceptions to my recommended order, but exceptions must be
received by the Commission within fifteen days after the recommended order is issued.
See § 110.227(6), Fla. Stat. (2015); Fla. Admin. Code Rule 28- 106.104 and 28-
106.217(1). The Commission may not change the findings of fact or mitigation
recommendation (if any) in this order without first reviewing an official transcript of the
hearing. Any party who desires the Commission to review the transcript must file one
along with the exceptions.
